The 'residence with life care agreement' gave, 'in consideration for the payment of an initial entry fee, plus a monthly maintenance fee,' housing, food and health care, and 'specifies that the document does not create a landlord/tenant relationship.'
'the lack of a residential lease precludes application of the constructive eviction concept to this case'; the demurrer in the facility's favour was affirmed on every count.

Appellee is 'pennswood village, a nonprofit continuing care facility for individuals over the age of sixty-five' whose premises 'include resident apartments ... guest housing, and two special care facilities.'
'defendants agreed to rent premises in a two family, owner-occupied dwelling for a two-year period' and later invoked the Rent Security Deposit Act.
'a tenant in owner-occupied premises may invoke the provisions of the rent security deposit act at any time during the tenancy'; the judgment for possession was vacated and the complaint dismissed.
The letting was of one of not more than two rental units in the landlords' own 'two family, owner-occupied dwelling.'
Municipal ordinances 'imposing additional restrictions on the freedom of landlords within the municipality to raise rents' for residential apartments.

'the renting of residential property is as much an essential enterprise as the retail sale of food-stuffs ... and equally subject to public regulation when the need arises'; the judgment striking the West Orange ordinance was reversed and the Wayne ordinance upheld.
Plaintiffs are apartment-complex owners and partnerships whose proof was 'the affidavit of richard segal, manager of apartments owned by plaintiff-intervenors.'

Dismissed on procedure alone - 'the plaintiffs have a plain, adequate, and complete remedy at law' before the board of appeals - and the grievance was that 'they cannot sell their land for the construction of new buildings for hotel purposes,' no question of letting rooms being decided.
Suit on a one-year lease of 'a certain apartment known as b3, no. 240 south connecticut avenue, atlantic city' after the tenant moved out early.

'to constitute a surrender by agreement the parties should have executed a written release ... no such situation was created by the alleged agreement in this case, and the judgment [for the tenant] must therefore be reversed.'
The plaintiff took an assignment of the lease, 'took over the possession of the apartment-house,' and 'as owner and lessor, had refused to accept a surrender.'

Owners of adjoining lots were 'restrained from carrying out their declared purpose of erecting a four-story apartment house designed to contain thirty-six apartments' - a restriction on building for letting dwellings.

'The proposed construction was therefore declared a violation of the covenant, and the present plaintiffs in error were perpetually enjoined from constructing the flat or apartment building in question'; judgment affirmed.
Sadie Arnoff and the Clair-Doan Building & Construction Company had contracted to purchase lots 189 and 190 to erect a thirty-six apartment building, not to dwell there.
'The plaintiff let to the defendant an unfurnished dwelling, known as 334 West Fifty-eighth street, in the city of New York, for one year ... for $1,800' - compensated occupancy of a dwelling.
'The law does not imply a covenant on the part of the lessor that the dwelling is without inherent defects rendering it unfit for a residence'; judgment for the letting owner affirmed.
Maria L. Daly let the whole of the dwelling to the defendant, who 'began to occupy the premises' himself; the owner dealt with him only through her agent.

The suit is over jewelry stolen from safe-deposit boxes - 'a hotel will not be availed of limited liability provided by section 200 ... unless the hotel establishes that it provided a "safe"' - a hotel tort with no letting question decided.
Summary dispossess of residential tenants: 'no lessee or tenant ... may be removed ... except upon the establishment of one of the following grounds as good cause.'

'An owner of property ... once he accepts a tenant on that property, no longer has a right of possession to it'; the landlord's dispossess action was dismissed for failure to comply with the good-cause notice.
The landlord is the corporation '25 Fairmount Avenue, Inc.,' letting residential premises under a year-to-year lease; no owner occupancy appears.
The opinion decides only that 'a second notice and demand after the termination of the tenancy is not required' for jurisdiction, and never identifies the premises as a dwelling or rooms.
Convictions were for 'failing to secure a rental license for each of the rental properties' where 'there are tenants residing in each of the properties' - direct regulation of letting dwellings.
'The city lacked the express, implied and necessary power to enact the provisions in the ordinance to withhold licenses ... the judgment of sentence is reversed, and Sandra Hoffman is discharged.'
'Hoffman owns seven properties ... There are tenants residing in each of the properties' on oral month-to-month leases; the ordinance itself addresses 'non-owner occupied and rental properties.'
'Lien law ... gives a boarding house keeper a lien on property brought on the premises by a guest' for board furnished to a husband, wife and son who 'became boarders at a boarding house.'
'Mrs. Davis ... acquired a lien upon the piano for the board which she was furnishing from day to day'; judgment reversed in favor of the boarding-house keeper's claim.
The family 'became boarders at the boarding house of Mrs. Jane Davis in Albany, and he brought with him the piano and furniture for his rooms.'
'The foregoing claim is for boarding and lodging plaintiff's testator and family at the tavern of defendant' - the lawfulness of the keeper's charge for board and lodging.

'He also practised the lawful business of a boardinghouse keeper, which could not be rendered illegal by the fact that transient guests were received'; the unlicensed keeper could recover his board bill.
The goods 'were detained by the defendant, being in his house, the United States Hotel, until the above claim for boarding should be paid.'
The rule at issue provides 'nonresident owners, whose units are rented or available for rent, do not have the use of the recreational facilities' - a burden attached to letting one's dwelling.
'A conveyance of the unit to a tenant necessarily suspends the owner's access to the common area for the length of the tenancy'; the restriction and the fines against the letting owner were upheld.
'Liebler never lived in the unit, but leased it to his daughter and then to a succession of tenants.'
'The ordinance prohibits the removal of any controlled rental unit unless the city rent control board issues a permit' - direct regulation of rental dwellings.

'Removal permits were required in order to combine physically the units in question, and ... the two properties remain subject to the local rent control provisions'; judgment for the board affirmed with double costs.

The opinion establishes only that the properties 'have historically been rented as eight rental units' and rejects the plaintiffs' claim of exemption as 'owner-occupied three-family' houses without finding where the owners lived.
'A landlord seized his tenant's goods in execution for defaulted rental payments of an apartment' under a lease letting the apartment to her.
'The landlord, having the right to reenter and repossess premises for default in rents by the terms of the lease, had implied authority to remove furniture'; judgment for the owner affirmed.
The lessor is the Chelten Avenue Building Corporation, which by the lease 'may thereupon re-let the demised premises and cancel the certificate for the accompanying shares of stock.'
A three-year lease of an apartment at $125 a month was 'recontrolled' so that 'the rent which could lawfully be exacted was only such previously established maximum rent.'
'All that the lessor was entitled to receive for the use and occupancy of the apartment by the lessee was a rental not exceeding $55 a month'; the owner's constitutional and rescission claims failed.
'At the time the property was leased to the defendant, it had been occupied by the owner for the twenty-four month period' - she moved out and let the whole apartment.
'The action was on a lease for the rent of dwelling apartments in the building 321 Bank street' - compensated occupancy of a dwelling.
'The conduct of the landlord becomes evidence of an eviction in answer to his claim for rent accruing after such removal'; judgment against the letting owner affirmed.

'A landlord, who has rented part of his building to a tenant as a dwelling, permits another part to be used for lewd purposes' - he lets apartments in the building, with no residence of his own shown there.
Tenants in a 142-unit apartment building sued over sanitary-code provisions 'governing charges for utilities' in their dwelling units.
'Kennedy Lofts' system of charges for heating, cooling, and hot water in the building is inconsistent with the requirements of the regulation'; summary judgment entered against the landlord.
'Kennedy Lofts Associates Limited Partnership ... owns and operates the building' and lets its 142 apartments through a management agent.

The decision turns entirely on the roomer's own conduct - 'the plaintiff with full knowledge of all the facts proceeded to use an unlighted stairway' - a personal-injury case with no letting question decided.

'Flats or floors of a house, when leased separately to tenants, are as much separate dwellings as adjoining houses,' and the plaintiff's 'business ... as the keeper of a lodging-house was injured' when 'her lodgers forsook their rooms.'

'As against their tenant they could not do the same thing, even in the most careful manner, if the result destroyed the quiet enjoyment of such tenant'; the letting owners were held liable irrespective of negligence.

The defendants let the third and fourth floors of 105 Stockton Street to the plaintiff, the rule being that a letting creates a tenancy 'if the owner does not reside as such on the premises, or retain control of the whole.'
'The premises was a single-room occupancy (SRO) hotel' housing 131 residents, and the court enforced the housing maintenance code against its owners.

'A vacate order issued to insure the safety of the tenants and others should not be used as a pretext for permanently reducing the housing stock'; the owners' objections were rejected and the access and repair orders stood.
The respondents own and run the SRO hotel at 341 Broome Street, whose 'recent purchase of the property involved more than $1,000,000,' and whose 'ultimate goal' the court found to be demolition.
The duty at issue arises from 'the rental agreement signed by the Rowletts' for 'the house appellants were renting from appellee,' including its repair and exculpatory clauses.

'This raises fact issues as to whether, first, Mr. McMillan had a duty to make repairs ... it was error for the trial judge to render a summary judgment for appellee'; the letting owner lost his judgment.
McMillan let the house to the Rowletts and 'did send a repair crew to the premises but then refused to authorize replacement of the door.'
The owners of a three-family house sought 'a certificate of exemption, on the basis of owner occupancy, from the town's rent and eviction control by-law.'
'The board properly made a deeper inquiry into that question in this case and ... had a reasonable basis to reject the plaintiffs' application'; the units stay under rent control.
'The plaintiff Michael Lebner is not an occupant of the house. Lebner is in the business of owning and managing property,' and the resident's ownership was found to be a straw.
'The San Francisco rent ordinance requires an owner to reside for 12 months in an apartment that has been vacated pursuant to an "owner move-in" eviction notice.'
'Section 37.9(f) represents a proper exercise of the concomitant power to set appropriate penalties'; the treble-damage judgment for wrongful eviction against the owner was affirmed.
'Appellant purchased an apartment building at 76 Deming Street in March 1986' and evicted tenants; 'although appellant did move into the vacated apartment, he lived there for less than three months.'
A holdover proceeding against a tenant of a 'HUD section 202 senior citizen housing unit' for permitting her adopted daughter 'to occupy the premises without petitioner's prior written approval.'
'The occupancy restrictions in the lease on the facts here cannot support termination of the tenancy ... the petition is dismissed'; the owner's control over who may occupy was cut back.
Greene Avenue Associates owns the subsidized apartment building at 80 Greene Avenue and lets its units through 'AMS Realty Company, petitioner's managing agent.'
The indictment is for suffering 'the game of cock-fighting' in a licensed house under a statute forbidding gaming implements; nothing is decided about lodging or the letting of rooms.
'Whether the landlord's failure to provide its tenants with adequate security breaches the warranty of habitability' in a residential nonpayment proceeding.
'The landlord's failure to adequately protect its tenants' security breaches the warranty of habitability,' and the tenant's counterclaims were allowed despite the lease waiver.
The petitioner is '610 W. 142nd St. Owners Corp.,' the successor owner of the apartment building, acting through 'one of petitioner's agents, a Morris Scharf.'
Zoning denial for a dwelling to be occupied by 12 unrelated residents who 'would pay a certain percentage of their income' for room, board and services.
'The borough may not arbitrarily limit the use of single-family dwellings only to persons related by blood, adoption or marriage ... the appeal of Group Home, Inc., is sustained.'
'Group Home, Inc., has agreed to purchase the premises at 80 South Wade Avenue,' and 'the one or two counselors would not occupy the premises overnight as residents.'
Challenge to regulations 'enlarging the class of "family members" entitled to succeed to a rent-regulated apartment on the death or departure of the tenant of record.'
'The regulations are within the agency's rule-making authority, and ... no unconstitutional "taking" was effected'; the owners' challenge failed and the succession restriction stands.

The appellants are the Rent Stabilization Association of New York City and Small Property Owners of New York, landlords of rent-regulated apartments who complained that the rules 'impose the social burden of housing selected classes of persons on individual landlords.'
"to board of defendant with plaintiff from 1889 to 1894 intermittently, and board from 1894 to 1904 as per agreement" - the suit is for the price of board furnished in the plaintiff's home.

Judgment affirmed for the householder who furnished the board: "they met and settled their differences by adjusting the indebtedness of one to the other at the sum of $500, which the debtor then and there agreed to pay."
"the plaintiff, a builder residing at bayonne, arranged with the defendant, his aunt, to reside with him" - board furnished in the plaintiff's own household.
"gorsuch homes, inc., d.b.a. villa park, ltd., is the owner of the apartment complex, villa park, where wooten is a tenant under section 8 federally subsidized housing."
"judgment is entered in wooten's favor on the issue of her eviction from the premises" - the owner's eviction failed and due-process limits were imposed on terminating the tenancy.
The letting party is a corporate owner of an apartment complex acting through a resident manager and a regional property manager, not an occupant of the premises.

"he made arrangements with robert novick to rent the farm dwelling house near sinton on a month to month basis ... novick was to pay appellant $75.00 per month rent" - the case turns on the dwelling being let rather than owner-occupied.

"the summary judgment proof conclusively establishes, as a matter of law, that appellant, the insured, was not occupying the house principally for dwelling purposes" - coverage was forfeited because he let it, and "a higher premium is charged for the tenant occupied dwelling."
"neither he nor his wife judith went to or entered the dwelling house after novick started occupying it" - the owner had moved away and let the whole house.

The dispute is over "this office of approximately 300 square feet" rented to the natural life medical center and two commercial sign variances - office space, not compensated occupancy of a dwelling or rooms.

"no public entity ... shall, by statute, ordinance, or regulation ... compel the owner of any residential real property to offer, or to continue to offer, accommodations in the property for rent or lease."

"we conclude sections 1806 and 1803 are invalid to the extent they conflict with the ellis act by prohibiting residential landlords from evicting tenants in order to go out of the rental residential housing business."
"respondent landlords" are owners of santa monica apartment buildings subject to rent control, not occupants of them.

The only question decided is workmen's compensation coverage: "the commission found that robinson's employment was casual, but that it was in the usual course of the business or occupation of the petitioner" - the lodging house is merely the employer's business, with no letting question.
"defendant is a long term tenant of plaintiff in its federally subsidized low income housing project in jersey city" - a residential tenancy and the statutory grounds for removal.
"reversed and remanded for entry of an order vacating the judgment of possession" - the landlord's removal of the tenant under its no-pet rule was undone.
The letting party is "jersey city management," operator-owner of a low income housing project, not a resident of the unit.
"lessor does hereby demise and let unto lessee all that certain first-floor apartment, 35 s. morton ave., morton, pa." - the terms of a residential letting are what the court construes.

"the exculpatory provisions are not 'beyond doubt by express stipulation,' and as a matter of law are not exculpatory" - the landlord's immunity clause failed, and the court added that "the contract is one of adhesion."
The defendant is the landlord of an apartment building who "specifically extended his protection to the entire building" of apartments let to tenants.

"at the time of the fire, 18 apartments had been purchased by shareholders, 26 were rented as rent-stabilized or controlled apartments and the remainder were rented at unregulated market rates" - the housing maintenance code duty of an owner of let dwellings.

"as 'owners' of the premises under the hmc, appellants are obligated to undertake and finance the restoration of the premises" and "the trial court's order to repair does not constitute an unconstitutional physical or regulatory taking."
"they also acted as landlords to the nonshareholder tenants" - controlling shareholders and the managing agent of the building, not occupants letting their own home.

"a dwellinghouse is a protection from arrest upon civil process to the occupant, his children, and domestic servants, and to permanent boarders or lodgers" - the legal character of boarding in a householder's dwelling.

"permanent boarders, or those who have made the house their home, may properly be considered as a part of the family" - the householder's castle was extended to the man he boarded; he lost only on a pleading defect unrelated to letting.
"chase was at the time, and had been for a long time before, a lodger and boarder in the house of the plaintiff" - the plaintiff occupied the house and took in the boarder.

"the plaintiff became a guest of the defendant's hotel, and contracted a bill amounting to $37.95, which being unpaid, his baggage ... was retained as security" - the innkeeper's lien for the board bill is the subject.

"the authority to sell, not being derived from compliance with the statute, nor from the judgment or decree of any court, must have come from the plaintiff, or otherwise it was unauthorized and amounts in law to a conversion" - verdict of $205 against the hotel-keeper.
"the defendant, being a hotel-keeper, had an inn-keeper's lien upon the plaintiff's baggage" - a hotel kept as a business.
"in september 1988, mr. perez and his family moved into a regular two-bedroom apartment at the complex" at a discounted rent - a residential tenancy under the summary dispossess statute.
"the facts of this case unequivocally leads to the conclusion that njsa 2a:18-61.1(m) is inapplicable. therefore, the complaint for possession is dismissed."
The letting party is "the apartment complex owned by the plaintiff," village associates, letting units through employees rather than living there.
"an excise is hereby imposed upon the transfer of occupancy of any room or rooms in a bed and breakfast establishment, hotel, lodging house, or motel" - the taxation of paid room occupancy.

"g. l. c. 64g, by its terms, does not impose a room occupancy excise on rent paid by individuals who remain longer than ninety consecutive days as guests" - the tax on the operators' letting was narrowed and abatement allowed.
"plaintiffs, charles and irene lowney, own and operate the carleton circle motel (motel) in falmouth" with thirty-eight units let to short- and long-term guests.

The question is whether the property is "a unit or units in an owner-occupied two-family or three-family house" exempt from "st. 1976, c. 36, the cambridge rent control act" - the regulation of residential letting.
"the property is, at the present time, a four-family building and is subject to rent control" - the exemption was construed narrowly against the owner and rent control upheld over his units.
"martin, his wife, and two children moved into unit two at 111 henry street ... while continuing to rent the two units at 109 henry street to tenants" - an owner living in the building he lets.

"it was conceded upon the trial that from september, 1946, the tenant used the apartment as a home for himself and his family" and the administrator found "the predominant use was for dwelling purposes" under the state residential rent law.

"the determination appealed from should be reversed and a new trial granted, with costs to appellant" - the landlord's award of possession was undone so the tenant could prove the lease "was a subterfuge for the purpose of evasion ... of the applicable rent control laws."
The letting party is 97 fifth avenue corporation, which "acquired title to the premises" and let the apartment, not an occupant of the building.
"the defendant had impliedly undertaken as a part of the letting to keep the hallway lighted" - a duty arising out of the contract of letting an apartment.
"there was no error in denying the defendant's motion for a directed verdict" - the owner who let was held liable for the unlit common hallway.
"an apartment on the first floor of a two family house owned by the defendant, who occupied the second floor apartment" - the owner lived in the house he let.
"this was an action of indebitatus assumpsit for the use and occupation of a certain piece of land, and a house standing thereon" - what is owed for occupying another's house.

"indebitatus assumpsit can be supported, on the implied promise arising merely from use and occupation of real estate by permission" - a new trial granted so the owner may recover for the occupancy of his house without an express lease.

"the defendant ... went into the possession, use and occupation of the premises under the plaintiff, and by his permission; and from that time ... took all the rents and profits to himself" - the owner was out of possession.
"he was received as a guest, and the innkeeper took charge of his property" - the incidents of the innkeeper-guest relation, including the lien for charges, are what the court defines.

"the defendant, if he will keep an inn, ought, at his peril, to keep safely his guests' goods" - judgment affirmed against the innkeeper as insurer, a burden laid on the calling of receiving guests for pay.
"the landlord, who fixes his own measure of compensation, and holds the property in pledge for the payment of his charges" - an inn kept as a public vocation.

"defendants, the sanborns, leased to mr. and mrs. kendis an apartment house in los angeles city consisting of twenty-five furnished apartments for a term of ten years" - the terms on which dwelling accommodations are let.
"the lessors could fix any terms of payment for giving their consent that they saw fit"; judgment affirmed for the owners, upholding their control over transfers of the letting.
The sanborns owned and let the twenty-five-unit furnished apartment house to lessees who held and assigned it; they did not occupy it.

"located on the premises were a small hotel, a barber shop and beauty shop, a printing shop and a portion of the said lots was subrented and used for other purposes" - a commercial rental contract of mixed business realty, decided on rent default and trespass to try title.
"included in the trust estate were four loft buildings" let to "thirty tenants" of commercial loft space - a gross receipts tax on commercial rentals, not on letting dwellings or rooms.

"whenever a lease of residential property shall provide that ... the landlord may recover attorneys' fees" there shall be implied a like covenant for the tenant - the regulation of the residential letting relation under rent control.

"real property law section 234 applies to a statutory tenant under the rent control law even if not a signatory to the lease ... and ... the statute applies retroactively" - $51,517.25 in fees charged against the owners after their eviction attempt failed.
Petitioners are "the owners of the washington square north property ... as executors of the estate of manny duell," letting a rent-controlled apartment they do not occupy.
"plaintiff's agent was not a guest nor did he intend to become one ... under these facts he was not a guest" - a checkroom bailment claim by a non-guest, with no question about the letting of rooms.

"their purpose in buying the property was to convert an existing house on the property into a two-family dwelling and offer both apartments for rent," which "would violate a zoning ordinance concerning minimum lot size per family."

"we hold as a matter of law that the facts of this case show the expenditure of substantial unrecoverable sums and we reverse the trial court" - the zoning denial was reversed and the owners kept their two rental units.
The koziels bought the property to convert it and "offer both apartments for rent"; nothing shows them occupying either unit.

"samaritan inns is a tax-exempt charitable corporation that provides below-market rental housing" and "the district issued the demolition and building permits necessary to allow samaritan inns to renovate tabitha's house and operate it as a boarding house."

"the district does not contest the district court's finding that it violated the act by issuing an illegal stop-work order," and both boarding and rooming houses are "uses that are permitted as of right in the area where tabitha's house is located" - the regulatory obstruction of the letting was struck down.
Samaritan inns operates three "inns" and two "houses" letting rooms for compensation, and holds a certificate of occupancy "for its use as a rooming and boarding house."

The question is "whether the owner of a thirty-six unit apartment building ... has a continuing obligation to make some of the apartments available at below market rents" - direct regulation of the rents at which dwellings may be let.

"the act requires an owner to maintain the units as affordable for as long as the housing is not in compliance with local zoning requirements, regardless of the terms of any attendant construction subsidy agreements."
The owner is ardemore apartments limited partnership, which "purchased the project from cedar street associates" and lets the thirty-six units.
"the word 'hotel' as used in the liquor tax law contemplates only such a structure as complies with section 30n of said statute" - the statutory requirements a room-letting house must satisfy.

"relator's building had only five bedrooms instead of six, one of which was materially deficient in floor area and air space ... was ground for refusing the certificate" - the writ was quashed and the owner's application denied.
The premises were run for the travelling public, and the intervening holder was organized "to carry on the business of hotel and innkeepers, restaurant keepers, caterers, etc."

"defendant, a 72-year-old woman separated from her husband, decided to take in a roommate for reasons, as she stated, of security, companionship and to help pay for the rent" - compensated occupancy of rooms in her dwelling.

Both novel issues were held: "the rent overcharge provisions of the rent stabilization law and code are applicable in this case which involves a rental situation between a tenant and a sublessee/roommate" (a restriction), yet "the amount of rent a tenant may charge a subtenant, in a partial sublet if within the legal limits, should be determined by the process of negotiation and bargaining between the parties ... and should not entail the intervention of the court" (the overcharge claim struck).
"she resides in a two-bedroom, rent-stabilized apartment located on the upper west side of manhattan" and let the master bedroom while living there.
Holdover proceeding over who may occupy a rent-controlled apartment: 'santo had entered into a written lease with the landlord-appellant whereby santo rented apartment 3-b for residential purposes.'

Owner won and the local eviction-certificate restriction was held to yield: 'the final order should be reversed... and final order directed for the landlord' because 'a landlord owner in normal times has the right to evict a tenant and any other claiming under him holding over against the will of the landlord.'
The letting party is the building's landlord, not an occupant: 'joseph h. hunt, landlord, appellant' who received the rent for 'the santo apartment.'
Suit to stop paid room-letting in a residence: 'the foxworths were renting an apartment, located upstairs from their unattached garage, to a rice university student for profit.'
The court enjoined the letting: 'we render judgment that appellees john h. foxworth and erna beth foxworth be enjoined from renting the garage apartment as a source of financial gain.'
Owners occupied the home and let a room on the premises: 'they occupy a home in southampton place' and 'have rented the room on three different occasions to rice university students.'

The court fixed the terms implied in a residential letting: 'in the rental of a dwelling unit... there is an implied agreement by the landlord that the rented unit complies with the minimum standards prescribed by building and sanitary codes.'

New liability was imposed on the letting owner: 'extension of the warranty to the ordinary residential tenancy at will... logically carries with it liability for personal injuries caused by a breach,' and the directed verdict for the landlord was reversed.
The defendant owned the rental building without occupying it: 'the plaintiff was the tenant of the third-floor apartment in a three-family house in dorchester owned by the defendant.'
Summary proceeding under the housing rent regulation aimed at an occupant who sublet furnished rooms: 'he arranged with mr. curtis to sublet part of the place with his furniture in it.'
The court recognised the freedom to let and dismissed the owner's petition: 'he can assign the lease, sublet all or part or underlet... accordingly d'elia had the right to sublet.'
The sublettor lived in the premises he let: 'the tenant has retained use of one room and so far as the evidence goes uses it as a dwelling part of the time.'

No letting question: the suit is a poor-law claim by a farmer against overseers for a pauper's keep - 'overseers of the poor of parker city, entered into a contract with john shaffer, a farmer, by which he undertook to board and keep a swedish woman' - the occupant paid nothing and no occupancy arrangement was characterised or regulated.
Zoning control of multiple letting: the owner 'sought... a certificate of variance to permit his property... to be used for a six-family dwelling.'

The restriction on letting was upheld: 'the decision of the board is affirmed; the appeal by writ of certiorari is dismissed,' since 'zoning regulation of open rear-yard space in so congested a neighborhood must be upheld... even though it works a hardship on mr. hinton.'
The owner runs the building as rented apartments rather than living in it: 'mr. hinton has been conducting the apartment house operation for several years.'

Criminal zoning charge for letting a house to several households: 'charging appellant... with a violation of the city's zoning code in using certain property, zoned r-2 single family residential, as a multifamily dwelling.'

The restriction was enforced against the owner: 'mr. sarver's use of the premises as a triplex (multifamily residential purpose) was not a legal nonconforming use. rather, it was an illegal use. he must be found guilty' - judgment affirmed.
The owner let all three units and did not live there: 'appellant rented the apartments to three unrelated families or persons.'
The case decides the validity of rent control over residential letting: 'the plaintiffs are tenants of rent-controlled housing accommodations in the defendant village of rockville centre.'

The court sustained decontrol and refused to reimpose the restriction: summary judgment was granted declaring 'that the order of decontrol issued by the state division of housing and community renewal here in question is valid.'
The owners are landlords of rent-controlled housing they let out: 'the defendants-intervenors (a group of landlords) cross-moved for summary judgment.'

Insurance warranty case, letting only as background description: 'compliance with his warranty is a condition precedent to any recovery upon the contract' - the court decided the effect of a broken fire-policy warranty, not the character or regulation of the boarding-house occupancy.
Dispute over a residential letting: 'the judgment was entered on a lease... for a certain brick dwelling known as 709 montclair street, pittsburgh... at a rental of $65 per month.'

The owner's letting contract was enforced as written: 'defendants admittedly being in default in the payment of the installments of rent due at the time, the entire rent at once became due and payable under the terms of the lease, and judgment was properly entered.'
The lessor let a whole dwelling he did not occupy, and controlled subletting: 'he did say that if they could get a responsible party to sub-let that he would agree to their sub-letting.'

Municipal regulation of rental housing on condominium conversion: 'certain tenants advised pia that they were terminating their lease pursuant to lakewood residential condominium ordinance section 1327.06(e)(1).'

The restriction on the letting owner was upheld: 'lrco 1327.06(e)(1) is valid, reasonable, and constitutional. therefore, because the tenants are entitled to vacate the premises without penalty, no actions to retain security deposits nor for claimed lost rents may be maintained.'
A corporate owner letting units in a building it does not occupy: 'the owner/landlord, professional investments of america, inc.' of 'the lake house, a high-rise complex in lakewood, ohio.'

Ordinance controlling whether dwellings must stay let: it requires 'that any unit which is a controlled rental unit on august 10, 1979, remain part of the rental housing stock of the city of cambridge.'

The restriction was upheld against the owners: 'a city ordinance which denied the owner of a condominium the right to occupy his unit if it was used for rental housing on the effective date of the ordinance did not constitute an unconstitutional deprivation of property' - 'we uphold the validity of the ordinance.'
The plaintiffs let units they do not occupy: 'eight citizens of cambridge who reside in apartments owned by one of the plaintiffs' intervened as defendants.

Rent-ceiling regulation of a let apartment: the action alleged 'rental overcharges by the defendant in violation of the emergency price control act of 1942, as amended, and the housing and rent act of 1947.'

The owner was held liable in treble damages for exceeding the permitted rent: 'defendant admits that she received the rents set out in each count of the complaint... the judgment under review will be affirmed.'

The opinion identifies the letting party only as the registering landlord of an apartment with shared facilities - 'bathroom & toilet shared by other tenants' - and says nothing about whether she lived in the building.

The court decided the legal character of a paid occupancy of a dwelling: 'the trial court granted respondents judgment for possession of the premises, finding a landlord-tenant relationship existed between respondents and appellant.'

The letting owners' possessory remedy was upheld: 'a single writing (the 1985 agreement) created both a tenancy in common and a lease between three of the cotenants as lessors (respondents) and the fourth cotenant as lessee' - judgments affirmed in all respects.
The lessors were excluded from the home they let: 'the parties stipulated that appellant exercised exclusive possession of the property, that respondents as cotenants could not enter the premises.'
The court classified boarding-house keeping as a regulated business: the statute 'applies to furniture used in a boarding-house kept by a married woman.'

The keeper lost her property for not meeting the statutory filing burden on that business: 'the case at bar is one which comes within the mischief which the statute was designed to remedy' - exceptions overruled, verdict for the attaching creditor.

She kept the boarding house as a business, taking pay even from her husband: 'the furniture was used in a boarding-house kept by the plaintiff; that her husband boarded with her, paying for his board.'
Permit control of short-term letting: 'they applied for a special use permit to allow rental of their home to summer tenants in 2009 under the city of oneonta summer transient occupancy ordinance.'

The denial of permission to let was left standing: 'adjudged that the petition is dismissed, as moot, without costs,' the court finding 'the controversy is moot given that the 2009 summer rental season... has long since passed.'
Owners live in the house they proposed to let: 'petitioners are the resident owners of a single-family victorian-era home on draper street.'

Proceeding over subletting of controlled dwelling space: 'it is claimed that the subletting is a violation of the terms of the tenancy,' and 'walter shepherd is a sublessee of dwelling space and resides in a portion of the demised premises.'

The owner's attempt to regain the space failed because the rent statute protects the occupants: 'the undertenants have been in possession since before the enactment of the control statute. thus, they are protected by the statute... final order for tenants dismissing petition.'
The letting party is the apartment-house owner: 'the landlord is the owner of premises 610 west end avenue, new york, new york.'
The case turns on the effect of letting a dwelling for hire: 'plaintiffs have, since moving into the new house, rented the little house to different parties for short periods of time.'

Letting cost the owners nothing: 'the facts are sufficient to sustain the findings of the trial court that there was no segregation intended, and the renting of the cottage was merely temporary, hence there was no abandonment' - the homestead exemption was preserved and the sale enjoined.

Resident owners let a small house standing in their own fenced home lot: 'when said small house was rented, only the house was rented, and the plaintiffs reserved the use of the yard for their chickens and calves and horses.'

Challenge to rent and eviction control over dwellings: the ordinance is 'intended to regulate residential rent increases in the city of berkeley and to protect tenants from unwarranted rent increases and arbitrary, discriminatory, or retaliatory evictions.'

The restrictions on letting were sustained: 'plaintiffs, a group of landlords... appeal from a judgment... holding defendants' rent control ordinance constitutional on its face. we substantially affirm the judgment' - only the severable retaliatory-eviction presumption was struck.
The challengers let out property they do not live in: 'plaintiffs, a group of landlords who own property in the city of berkeley,' the ordinance exempting 'certain small owner-occupied buildings.'
